findings.body: Recompilation fails, while an already compiled provider loads but fails with AbstractMethodError when provider detection invokes order(), preventing crypto initialization.
findings.failure_mode: Previously valid third-party SPI implementations can no longer participate in provider discovery.
findings.impact: Recompilation fails, while an already compiled provider loads but fails with AbstractMethodError when provider detection invokes order(), preventing crypto initialization.
findings.root_cause: The patch adds a required method to a public service-provider interface instead of evolving it with a default implementation.
findings.suggested_fix: Make order() a default interface method with a compatibility-safe priority, and assign the authz fallback a lower explicit priority than that default.
findings.title: Adding an abstract SPI method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.trigger: A downstream application loads a CryptoProvider implementation compiled against an earlier keycloak-common version or recompiles an implementation that has not added order().
findings.verifier_reason: Patch adds `int order();` at line 44 of CryptoProvider.java as an abstract method without a default implementation. Existing third-party implementations compiled against older versions will fail with AbstractMethodError when order() is invoked during provider detection. The patch context confirms DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, and WildFlyElytronProvider all add order() implementations, but external implementations would break.

findings.body: The first ServiceLoader entry is selected silently; a deployment intended to use FIPS can instead use the non-FIPS provider depending on resource/classpath ordering, whereas this configuration previously failed fast.
findings.failure_mode: An ambiguous crypto configuration starts with an unintended provider instead of reporting the conflict.
findings.impact: The first ServiceLoader entry is selected silently; a deployment intended to use FIPS can instead use the non-FIPS provider depending on resource/classpath ordering, whereas this configuration previously failed fast.
findings.root_cause: Multiple-provider rejection was removed without defining deterministic behavior for equal priorities.
findings.suggested_fix: After sorting, reject multiple providers tied for the highest order, or assign unique, semantically defined priorities; only permit lower-priority fallback providers to be ignored.
findings.title: Equal top priorities make full crypto-provider selection classpath-dependent
findings.trigger: Two full providers with the same order are visible, such as DefaultCryptoProvider and FIPS1402Provider, which are both assigned order 200.
findings.verifier_reason: Patch at line 57 shows `.sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order).reversed())` and removes the previous multi-provider rejection. DefaultCryptoProvider and FIPS1402Provider both return order 200 per the patch context, making selection classpath-dependent when both are present. This is a real behavioral change from fail-fast to silent arbitrary selection.

findings.body: Two encoder instances and two encoded integer byte arrays are created and immediately discarded, adding unnecessary allocation and obscuring the intended single encoding path.
findings.failure_mode: The hot conversion path performs redundant work with no observable result.
findings.impact: Two encoder instances and two encoded integer byte arrays are created and immediately discarded, adding unnecessary allocation and obscuring the intended single encoding path.
findings.root_cause: Intermediate encoder calls were left as dead statements instead of being used in the returned sequence.
findings.suggested_fix: Delete both discarded write calls; the subsequent writeDerSeq call already encodes both integers.
findings.title: Discarded ASN.1 encodings perform duplicate work on every conversion
findings.trigger: Any ECDSA concatenated-signature-to-DER conversion invokes these statements before constructing the actual sequence.
findings.verifier_reason: Lines 114-115 show `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` whose return values are discarded. The actual encoding happens at lines 117-121. These are dead statements performing redundant allocations.

pr.body:
…tory

closes #33831

This is the Keycloak main part for solving the https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/32962 and adding the related changes in the authz-client on the Keycloak side, which can then be later synced to the keycloak-client repository. 

In the end, I am using approach (2) from https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/32962 with adding the method `order()` to `CryptoProvider`, which allows to have multiple instances of `CryptoProvider` on classpath (Keycloak testsuite still uses the `DefaultCryptoProvider` as before this PR).

validated_findings.impact: Those tests do not exercise their mandated JOSE curves; in particular ES512 does not exercise 66-byte components or the long-form DER sequence lengths introduced by the new encoder and decoder.
validated_findings.root_cause: One unparameterized default EC key pair is shared across all three JOSE algorithms.
validated_findings.suggested_fix: Generate a curve-specific key for each algorithm using secp256r1, secp384r1, and secp521r1 respectively, preferably through a parameterized test.
validated_findings.title: ES384 and ES512 tests use a default P-256 key
validated_findings.trigger: The ES384 and ES512 test methods execute after the constructor generates the provider's default EC key, normally a 256-bit key, without selecting P-384 or P-521.
validated_findings.verifier_reason: Line 42 shows `keyPair = KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` which uses the default EC parameters (typically P-256). The same keyPair is used for ES256, ES384, and ES512 tests, so ES384/ES512 tests do not exercise their required curves (P-384, P-521) or the larger signature component sizes.

validated_findings.body: The round trip still returns its intermediate bytes and the test passes even though signatures emitted for or consumed from standards-compliant JOSE implementations are incorrect.
validated_findings.failure_mode: Mutually inverse implementation errors are invisible to the test suite.
validated_findings.impact: The round trip still returns its intermediate bytes and the test passes even though signatures emitted for or consumed from standards-compliant JOSE implementations are incorrect.
validated_findings.root_cause: The test compares two outputs produced exclusively by the same converter pair instead of checking either result against an independent expected value.
validated_findings.suggested_fix: Add known JOSE ECDSA vectors or independently validate the concatenated output and verify a converted signature using a separate JCA/standards implementation.
validated_findings.title: The conversion test has no independent interoperability oracle
validated_findings.trigger: Both conversion directions contain complementary defects, such as both swapping the r and s components or applying the same non-standard normalization.
validated_findings.verifier_reason: Line 56 shows `Assert.assertArrayEquals(rsConcat, rsConcat2)` which only verifies round-trip consistency. If both conversion directions have complementary bugs, the test passes while producing non-interoperable signatures. No independent oracle validates correctness.

validated_findings.body: Two encoder instances and two encoded integer byte arrays are created and immediately discarded, adding unnecessary allocation and obscuring the intended single encoding path.
validated_findings.failure_mode: The hot conversion path performs redundant work with no observable result.
validated_findings.impact: Two encoder instances and two encoded integer byte arrays are created and immediately discarded, adding unnecessary allocation and obscuring the intended single encoding path.
validated_findings.root_cause: Intermediate encoder calls were left as dead statements instead of being used in the returned sequence.
validated_findings.suggested_fix: Delete both discarded write calls; the subsequent writeDerSeq call already encodes both integers.
validated_findings.title: Discarded ASN.1 encodings perform duplicate work on every conversion
validated_findings.trigger: Any ECDSA concatenated-signature-to-DER conversion invokes these statements before constructing the actual sequence.
validated_findings.verifier_reason: Lines 114-115 show `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` whose return values are discarded. The actual encoding happens at lines 117-121. These are dead statements performing redundant allocations.

validated_findings.body: The direct-construction ECDSA tests still pass even though AuthzClient.create can fail to initialize crypto or install the wrong provider in the actual integration path.
validated_findings.failure_mode: CI cannot detect broken service metadata, class-loader discovery, or priority selection.
validated_findings.impact: The direct-construction ECDSA tests still pass even though AuthzClient.create can fail to initialize crypto or install the wrong provider in the actual integration path.
validated_findings.root_cause: The only new provider test instantiates the implementation directly and therefore does not cover the feature's registration and discovery mechanism.
validated_findings.suggested_fix: Add an isolated integration test that initializes through AuthzClient.create or CryptoIntegration.init, discovers the provider through ServiceLoader, and also verifies coexistence with a higher-priority full provider.
validated_findings.title: Tests bypass the newly added ServiceLoader registration and selection path
validated_findings.trigger: The service descriptor is missing or mispackaged, AuthzClient uses a class loader that cannot discover it, or provider ordering selects an unexpected implementation.
validated_findings.verifier_reason: Line 47 shows `AuthzClientCryptoProvider prov = new AuthzClientCryptoProvider()` which directly instantiates the provider, bypassing ServiceLoader discovery and CryptoIntegration.init. Missing service descriptors or incorrect priority ordering would not be detected by these tests.
